tower-of-hanoi.title: Goal Stack Ordering
tower-of-hanoi.principle: The final configuration on the goal peg must be a descending stack: the largest disk at the bottom, each smaller disk directly above a larger one, ending with the smallest on top. Any deviation from this order violates the Tower of Hanoi rules.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: Whenever you are checking whether the current or final state satisfies the problem’s goal, or before placing a disk onto the goal peg.
tower-of-hanoi.example: For 5 disks, the goal stack on peg 2 should be [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] from bottom to top.

tower-of-hanoi.title: Place Larger Disks Before Smaller
tower-of-hanoi.principle: Because a larger disk can never sit on a smaller one, any disk that must appear below another in the final stack must be moved onto the goal peg before the smaller disk that will sit on it. This ordering prevents illegal placements.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: When planning the sequence of moves that build the goal tower, always schedule the move of a larger disk before the move of any smaller disk that will sit on it.
tower-of-hanoi.example: Move disk 5 onto the goal peg before moving disk 4, and move disk 4 before moving disk 3, etc.

tower-of-hanoi.title: Free Blocked Disk
tower-of-hanoi.principle: A disk that has any smaller disks on top of it cannot be moved directly; you must first relocate those smaller disks to other pegs, respecting legality, before the blocked disk becomes the topmost disk and can be moved.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: Whenever the disk you need to move is not the top disk on its current peg.
tower-of-hanoi.example: To move disk 5 from peg 1, first move disk 1 and disk 4 (the disks above it) to other pegs.

tower-of-hanoi.title: Use Auxiliary Peg for Temporary Storage
tower-of-hanoi.principle: In a three‑peg problem, the peg that is neither the source nor the final destination of a move serves as a temporary holding area. It can store one or more smaller disks while larger disks are transferred.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: Whenever you need to free a blocked disk or need a place to hold a disk temporarily while moving another.
tower-of-hanoi.example: While moving disk 5 from peg 1 to peg 2, use peg 0 as the auxiliary peg to hold disks 1 and 4.

tower-of-hanoi.title: Recursive Sub‑tower Transfer
tower-of-hanoi.principle: Moving a stack of k disks from one peg to another follows the recursion: first move the top k‑1 disks to the auxiliary peg, then move the largest of the k disks to the target peg, and finally move the k‑1 disks from the auxiliary peg onto the target peg. This pattern yields the optimal sequence for a pure tower.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: Whenever you need to relocate a contiguous sub‑tower (multiple disks that are already ordered) as a unit.
tower-of-hanoi.example: To move disks 1‑3 from peg 0 to peg 2, first move disks 1‑2 to peg 1, move disk 3 to peg 2, then move disks 1‑2 onto peg 2.

tower-of-hanoi.title: Check Move Legality
tower-of-hanoi.principle: A legal move must take the topmost disk from the source peg and place it onto a destination peg whose top disk (if any) is larger than the moving disk, or onto an empty peg. Any move violating this rule is illegal.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: Before committing any move in your plan, verify that the source peg’s top disk is the one you intend to move and that the destination peg’s top (or emptiness) permits the placement.
tower-of-hanoi.example: Moving disk 4 onto a peg whose top disk is 2 is illegal because 4 > 2.

tower-of-hanoi.title: Simulate Final Configuration
tower-of-hanoi.principle: After you have written a complete move list, mentally replay each move from the initial state to ensure that every step is legal and that the final arrangement matches the goal configuration exactly. This catch‑all verification prevents hidden errors.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: After constructing the full sequence of moves, before outputting the answer.
tower-of-hanoi.example: Starting from the given initial stacks, step through each move in the list and confirm that the final peg 2 contains [5, 4, 3, 2, 1].

tower-of-hanoi.title: Maintain 0‑Indexed Peg Numbers
tower-of-hanoi.principle: The output format expects peg identifiers 0, 1, 2. Using any other numbering (e.g., 1‑based) will be parsed incorrectly and cause the answer to be rejected.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: When writing the final move list that will be parsed by the verifier.
tower-of-hanoi.example: To move a disk from the first peg to the third peg, write [disk, 0, 2] rather than [disk, 1, 3].

tower-of-hanoi.title: Track Current Top Disk on Each Peg
tower-of-hanoi.principle: Keep an up‑to‑date mental (or written) record of the topmost disk on every peg after each move. This prevents attempting to move a non‑top disk and helps you quickly decide which moves are legal.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: Continuously while constructing the move sequence.
tower-of-hanoi.example: After moving disk 1 from peg 1 to peg 2, update the top of peg 1 to be disk 4.

tower-of-hanoi.title: Leverage Existing Larger Disks on Target as Base
tower-of-hanoi.principle: If the goal peg already contains larger disks that are correctly placed (i.e., they match the final descending order), you can treat that peg as the base for the remaining smaller disks and avoid moving those larger disks again.
tower-of-hanoi.when_to_apply: When the target peg is not empty at the start of the problem, and its current stack matches the bottom portion of the desired final stack.
tower-of-hanoi.example: If peg 2 already has disk 5 at the bottom, you can start building the rest of the tower on top of it without moving disk 5 again.

tower-of-hanoi.description: Placing a larger disk onto a smaller one
tower-of-hanoi.why_it_happens: The model may forget the rule that larger disks cannot be placed on top of smaller ones, especially when focusing on moving a specific disk.
tower-of-hanoi.how_to_avoid: Always check the size of the destination peg’s top disk (or emptiness) before committing a move; if the destination top is smaller, the move is illegal.

tower-of-hanoi.why_it_happens: The model may lose track of the current stack order after many moves and try to move a disk that is buried under others.
tower-of-hanoi.how_to_avoid: Keep a running list of the top disk on each peg (or visualize the stacks) and only select moves that involve those top disks.

tower-of-hanoi.description: Prematurely placing a small disk on the goal peg
tower-of-hanoi.why_it_happens: The model may try to “park” the smallest disk early, forgetting that larger disks still need to be placed below it.
tower-of-hanoi.how_to_avoid: Remember the ordering principle (larger before smaller) and only place a small disk on the goal peg after all larger disks that belong beneath it have been positioned.

tower-of-hanoi.why_it_happens: The model may think in 1‑based terms while the verifier expects 0‑based indices.
tower-of-hanoi.how_to_avoid: Explicitly label the pegs as 0, 1, 2 in your notes and double‑check each move’s from‑peg and to‑peg numbers before writing them.

tower-of-hanoi.description: Skipping final verification of the goal state
tower-of-hanoi.why_it_happens: After constructing a long move list, the model may assume it is correct and omit a final mental replay.
tower-of-hanoi.how_to_avoid: After the move list is complete, replay the entire sequence from the initial configuration and confirm that the final stacks match the goal exactly.
